title: Star academic Peter Zandstra’s stem-cell startup Apiary Therapeutics has investors buzzing
html:
Scientist Peter Zandstra co-founded Apiary Therapeutics Ltd., a regenerative medicine startup that has raised $7.3-million.Justine Beaulieu-Poudrier/The Globe and Mail

Peter Zandstra had a few goals when he joined the University of British Columbia in 2016 to lead its new school of biomedical engineering. One of them was to turn more academics into entrepreneurs, building on UBC’s reputation as Canada’s premier source of biomedical spinouts.

It worked. Invention disclosures by the school’s academics nearly doubled in the 2026 fiscal year to 38 from four years earlier, and their research has spun out into 11 companies since April 2021.

“We have a responsibility to show value for the funding we get from government” and get medical innovations out of the lab and into the market, Dr. Zandstra said.

One of those spinouts is from Dr. Zandstra himself. On Monday, Apiary Therapeutics Ltd. – the fourth regenerative medicine startup he’s co-founded – is announcing it has raised $7.3-million, co-led by Toronto’s Genesys Capital and the Business Development Bank of Canada’s Life Sciences Venture Fund, and backed by InBC Investment Corp. and Cambridge, Mass.-based Mission BioCapital.

Dr. Zandstra, who became UBC’s vice-president of research and innovation in June, has led Apiary since its founding in 2023.

“It’s rare to work with a scientific founder who’s been entrepreneurial and started multiple companies,” said Genesys principal Sarah Farr. (Other Canadian academics-turned-entrepreneurs include Pieter Cullis, Molly Shoichet, Carl Hansen, Michael Hayden and Milica Radisic.) His experience as an entrepreneur and pioneering stem-cell bioengineering researcher – Dr. Zandstra previously led the University of Toronto’s Institute of Biomaterials and Biomedical Engineering – “will benefit the company.”

Apiary’s technology has worked on tissue samples in Petri dishes. Its next trial will determine if engineered B cells (a type of white blood cell that powers the immune system) implanted in mice can make disease-fighting proteins over prolonged periods.

Dr. Zandstra, who became UBC’s vice-president of research and innovation in June, has led Apiary since its founding in 2023.Justine Beaulieu-Poudrier/The Globe and Mail

If it works, and then again in humans, Apiary could transform how a range of conditions are treated. (Apiary hasn’t yet revealed its first target.) Instead of regular injections of therapeutic proteins, patients could receive a shot of supercharged cells once or twice a year that would continually administer the drug themselves inside their bodies. That should cut costs and increase effectiveness of treatments.

“We see Apiary’s technology as a step-change in how biologics can be dosed,” said Mission BioCapital partner Cynthia Lavoie.

“Nobody has really industrialized B cells yet,” said Parimal Nathwani, managing partner of the BDC fund. “We feel that’s the next wave of opportunity in cell therapy technologies.”

The 57-year-old Saskatchewan-born Dr. Zandstra has spent his career helping to commercialize Canadian discoveries. He was dismayed early on to see colleagues and students leave Canada for jobs in Boston. He was determined to create job opportunities for them here.

He co-founded his first company, an umbilical cord blood bank for stem cell transplantation, in 1996, four years before landing a professorship at the University of Toronto. (An Australian company bought the venture in 2016.) His second startup, ExCellThera, co-founded in 2015, continues to develop stem-cell therapies.

Dr. Zandstra co-founded the Centre for Commercialization of Regenerative Medicine in 2011 to bring cell and gene therapy manufacturing capabilities to Canada. It has helped launch or support more than a dozen companies.

On his watch, UBC’s biomedical engineering school launched a startup incubator and a program to teach entrepreneurship skills to students and staff. It struck an industry advisory board to shape curriculum. He even enhanced the evaluation system for his school so professors didn’t just report on their publications or grants, but also on whether they filed patents or started companies.

“Peter takes a more holistic view of what it means to really be innovative,” said Anna Blakney, an RNA vaccine researcher he recruited from the U.S. “Reframing those incentives or metrics for academics makes a huge difference.”

Since joining the school, Dr. Blakney has co-founded a company, something she said she likely wouldn’t have done without his encouragement.

Apiary is Dr. Zandstra’s second attempt at commercializing engineered white blood cells.

In more conventional cell therapies, doctors extract blood, bone marrow or tissue from patients. Samples are shipped to labs and manipulated to make them more potent before reinjection into patients – a costly, customized process.

Successful treatments of this sort have focused on T and NK white blood cells that destroy infected or abnormal cells, and blood cells for bone marrow transplants.

Notch Therapeutics, co-founded by Dr. Zandstra in 2018, instead derived a T-cell treatment from off-the-shelf stem cells that could be mass produced and delivered cost-effectively. Notch raised US$85-million in 2021 and hired 80 people, but it was caught out when the biotech funding market shut a year later. Notch wound down and was sold to giant Roche Holding AG.

“Notch was a disappointment,” he said. “We had so much momentum and such an opportunity to scale this company in Canada.”

Apiary takes a similar approach, but with B cells. Unlike other white blood cells that directly attack, B cells are like weapons factories, secreting proteins that then go on the offensive.

Apiary’s B cells are engineered to not only make specific proteins to target particular afflictions but also to avoid detection by the immune system as foreign objects. Once injected, the B cells should engraft in bone marrow and start producing their protein warheads.

Whether it works in living creatures isn’t yet known. “I’m excited about this platform based on the data we’ve generated,” Dr. Zandstra said. “I think it has legs.”
summary: UBC research VP-led company raises $7.3-million to turn engineered white blood cells into drug administering machines
